## Document Purpose

This master Software Requirements Specification consolidates the complete IMS requirements package into a single authoritative document. It covers business rules, use cases, domain model, system architecture, database design, REST API specifications, UI/UX specifications, and frontend architecture mapping.

## Scope

The Inventory Management System is an enterprise web application providing authoritative inventory truth across a multi-location network — covering product master data, procurement, inbound receiving, inventory control, order fulfillment, transfers, returns, reporting, governance, and administration.

## Delivery Phasing

| Phase | Timeline | Focus |
|-------|----------|-------|
| **MVP (Phase 1)** | Months 0–6 | Core visibility, movement recording, fulfillment support, audit |
| **Phase 2** | Months 6–12 | Network maturity, procurement automation, commercial campaigns |
| **Phase 3** | Months 12–18 | Finance alignment, executive analytics, advanced integrations |

This document establishes the **architectural direction** for the Inventory Management System — the principles, drivers, quality priorities, risks, and recommended style that will guide subsequent solution architecture, technology decisions, and detailed design. It answers *why* and *what kind of system* we are building at a strategic level, not *how each component is built*.

## 1. Architectural Goals

Architectural goals translate business intent into enduring design principles. They guide trade-off decisions throughout the 18-month initiative and beyond.

### AG-01 — Single Authoritative Source of Inventory Truth

Establish **Inventory Balance** as the system's quantity authority — one coherent answer to *what do we have, where is it, and what is available?* — consumable by all operational and management stakeholders without manual reconciliation across locations or parallel tools.

*Grounding:* BRD Executive Summary; BO-01, BO-03, BO-22; SRS-DM-009 (core domain identification); 13 bounded contexts with Inventory Balance at center of context map.

### AG-02 — Domain-Aligned Modularity

Organize the solution around **13 bounded contexts** identified in strategic domain design, preserving distinct ubiquitous languages, ownership boundaries, and change velocities — so catalog governance, warehouse execution, and financial controls can evolve independently without corrupting quantity invariants.

*Grounding:* SRS-DM-007; independence principles (distinct language, separate ownership, autonomous consistency).

### AG-03 — Governed Correctness Over Raw Speed

Enforce business rules — ATP commitment, put-away before availability, segregation of duties, approval thresholds, audit trail — as **architectural invariants**, not optional validations. Operational throughput must not come at the cost of ungoverned stock mutations.

*Grounding:* 32 business rules (BR-001 – BR-032); 20 SoD rules; NFR-COM-008, NFR-COM-009, NFR-SEC-007; event storming policies (POL-xxx).

### AG-04 — Phased Delivery With Credible Control

Deliver **measurable business control in Phase 1 (Months 0–6)** — core visibility, movement recording, fulfillment support, and audit — before pursuing network maturity, commercial campaigns, and financial alignment in later phases. Architecture must support incremental location rollout without operational shutdown (OC-01).

*Grounding:* BRD phased vision; MVP functional requirements; MoSCoW prioritization; ~122 Must Have NFRs.

### AG-05 — Event-Transparent Operations

Make every material inventory state change **observable, attributable, and reconstructable** through domain events and audit projections — enabling movement history, KPI dashboards, compliance evidence, and finance reconciliation without coupling reporting queries to transactional write paths.

*Grounding:* 81 domain events; Inventory Intelligence as event-consuming read context; BO-19; NFR-LOG, NFR-COM-010.

### AG-06 — Integration-Ready Enterprise Capability

Position IMS as the inventory system of record while **respecting external system boundaries** — Sales/CRM for customer orders, Finance/GL for valuation and payment — through explicit anti-corruption layers rather than absorbing foreign domain models.

*Grounding:* BRD scope exclusions; SRS-DM-007 context map (EXT Sales/CRM, EXT Finance); HS-014 Finance System Boundary.

### AG-07 — Scale Without Architectural Replacement

Design for **15% near-term and 30% medium-term growth** in orders, locations, SKUs, and users without forcing a rewrite — through capacity-aware core design, separable read workloads, and decomposition-ready module boundaries.

*Grounding:* NFR-SCAL-001 – NFR-SCAL-003; long-term business vision (3–5 years); NFR-SCAL-019 (no major replacement within 36 months).

### AG-08 — Resolve Domain Uncertainty Before Implementation

Treat **16 open event-storming hotspots** and **6 Priority-1 domain model findings** as architecture gate items — not implementation deferrals. Structural forks (lot/batch model, freeze authority, reservation coordination) must be closed before detailed design of affected capabilities.

*Grounding:* SRS-ES-007; SRS-DM-009 P1 items; Domain Model Review readiness gate.

## 2. Architectural Drivers

Architectural drivers are the forces that most strongly shape structural and technology decisions. They originate from domain complexity, NFR pressure, and delivery constraints.

### 2.1 Domain Structure Drivers

| Driver ID | Driver | Architectural Implication |
|-----------|--------|---------------------------|
| AD-01 | **Central quantity authority with many consumers** — Stock Position is mutated by receiving, fulfillment, transfers, adjustments, returns, and campaigns | Inventory Balance context must be isolated, highly consistent, and optimized for write contention; other contexts interact via commands, domain services, and events — not shared mutable state |
| AD-02 | **81 domain events across 12 transactional lifecycles** — event storming reveals rich cross-aggregate choreography (receipt→put-away→availability, confirm→reserve→pick→ship) | Internal **event-driven coordination** between bounded contexts; policies react to events rather than synchronous cross-module calls for non-immediate outcomes |
| AD-03 | **13 bounded contexts with heterogeneous change velocity** — catalog changes quarterly; balance changes continuously; governance changes on audit cycles | **Modular boundaries** aligned to contexts; avoid monolithic data model that couples master data to high-frequency transactions |
| AD-04 | **24 domain services spanning aggregates** — availability confirmation, reservation coordination, freeze guard, network availability evaluation | Cross-context **domain services and sagas** for workflows that cannot complete within a single aggregate transaction |
| AD-05 | **Inventory Intelligence as read-only projection context** — dashboards, KPIs, movement history, audit trail, valuation snapshots | **CQRS separation** — transactional write models distinct from read-optimized projections fed by domain events |
| AD-06 | **Governance and SoD as first-class concerns** — counter ≠ approver; adjustment thresholds; reason codes mandatory | **Policy enforcement layer** consulting Inventory Governance and Identity & Access before operational mutations; not ad hoc per-screen checks |
| AD-07 | **External system boundaries** — customer orders from Sales/CRM; financial authority potentially in ERP | **Anti-corruption layers** at Order Fulfillment and Inventory Intelligence boundaries; published interchange language (SKU, Location Code, User Identifier) |

### 2.2 Non-Functional Drivers

| Driver ID | Driver | Architectural Implication |
|-----------|--------|---------------------------|
| AD-08 | **Sub-3-second operational response** (NFR-PERF-001) and **sub-2-second ATP lookup** (NFR-PERF-002) | Hot-path read and write paths must minimize cross-context synchronous chains; ATP queries served from optimized read path or balance context with minimal fan-out |
| AD-09 | **99.5% business-hours uptime** for essential functions (NFR-AVL-001); peak 99.7% (NFR-AVL-003) | Resilience patterns for core transactional paths; graceful degradation for reporting; no single non-critical dependency blocking dock operations |
| AD-10 | **≤15-minute recovery point** for transactions (NFR-BDR-001, NFR-REL-007) | Durable event and transaction log; backup architecture aligned to stock balance and open reservations as critical data |
| AD-11 | **204 NFRs with ~122 Must Have** — security, logging, monitoring, compliance intertwined | **Cross-cutting platform capabilities** (auth, audit, observability) as shared infrastructure serving all contexts — not reimplemented per module |
| AD-12 | **7-year retention and immutable audit trail** (NFR-COM-006, NFR-COM-010, NFR-COM-020) | Tiered data architecture — hot operational store, warm audit store, cold archive — influencing projection and logging design |
| AD-13 | **Sequential multi-location rollout** (NFR-SCAL-007, OC-01) | Location-scoped configuration and phased feature enablement; architecture supports per-location go-live without network-wide cutover |
| AD-14 | **Concurrent reservation contention on high-velocity SKUs** (HS-007, NFR-PERF-007) | Optimistic or serialized reservation strategy on Stock Position; explicit saga compensation when order confirmation and reservation diverge |

### 2.3 Delivery and Constraint Drivers

| Driver ID | Driver | Architectural Implication |
|-----------|--------|---------------------------|
| AD-15 | **Fixed initiative budget** (BC-01) | Favor **modular monolith or minimal service count** for MVP; defer distributed-system complexity until proven scale or team capacity demands it |
| AD-16 | **Limited internal IT capacity** (ORC-04) | Reduce operational surface area — fewer deployable units, standardized observability, managed platform services where feasible |
| AD-17 | **No offline MVP** (TEC-03) | Online-first design; warehouse mobility via connected clients; no sync-engine architecture in Phase 1 |
| AD-18 | **No operational shutdown for go-live** (OC-01) | Parallel run, opening balance certification (HS-002), and rollback-capable deployment; architecture supports data migration and cutover modes |
| AD-19 | **Open hotspots blocking MVP rules** — ad-hoc receipt (HS-001), opening balance (HS-002), lot/batch model (HS-005) | Architecture sign-off gated on hotspot resolution workshops; assumptions documented where Phase 2 deferral is accepted |

|----------|-------------------|------------------|------------------|
| **1 — Critical** | **Data Integrity & Consistency** | NFR-REL-006–010; BR-001, BR-002, BR-005; DE-011–DE-022 | Strong consistency within Stock Position aggregate; eventual consistency across contexts with explicit compensation; no dual writers of ATP |
| **2 — Critical** | **Security & Compliance** | NFR-SEC (32); NFR-COM (22); FR-081–FR-090 | Centralized authN/authZ; location-scoped RBAC; immutable audit; GDPR and financial retention |
| **3 — Critical** | **Availability & Recoverability** | NFR-AVL-001 (99.5%); NFR-BDR-001 (15-min RPO); NFR-REL-001–005 | HA for essential functions; backup of balances and reservations; defined RTO scenarios |
| **4 — High** | **Performance (Operational)** | NFR-PERF-001 (3s screens); NFR-PERF-002 (2s ATP); NFR-PERF-003 (5s txn confirm) | Separate hot read paths; minimize cross-context sync in user-facing flows; index strategy for SKU/location lookup |
| **5 — High** | **Auditability & Traceability** | NFR-LOG (28); NFR-COM-010–014; BO-19 | Append-only movement and audit projections; 7-year retention tier; 15-minute auditor export (NFR-PERF-026) |
| **6 — High** | **Scalability** | NFR-SCAL-001–003; NFR-SCAL-010–015 | Horizontal scaling readiness for read tier; product-location aggregate partitioning; growth headroom without replacement |
| **7 — Medium** | **Observability** | NFR-MON (26); NFR-LOG-026 | Unified metrics, alerts, and runbooks; reservation failure and ATP contention visibility |
| **8 — Medium** | **Maintainability & Evolvability** | AD-03, AD-15; bounded context boundaries | Modular codebase aligned to contexts; published integration contracts; hotspot resolution before entrenchment |
| **9 — Medium** | **Usability (Operational)** | BO-21 (90% adoption); warehouse role differentiation | Role-appropriate UX; sub-3s response to prevent manual workaround reversion |
| **10 — Lower (Phase 2–3)** | **Reporting Performance** | NFR-PERF-023–027; NFR-AVL-004 | Async report generation; materialized KPI views; reporting outage must not block dock |

### 4.3 NFR-Driven Architectural Constraints

The NFR review identified constraints that architecture must explicitly address:

| Constraint | Source | Architectural Response |
|------------|--------|------------------------|
| Numeric conflicts between availability budgets and uptime percentages | NFR Review C-01 | Harmonize SLA definitions in capacity model before build |
| Aggressive RPO/RTO vs. fixed budget | NFR Review; BC-01 | Scenario-based DR tiers — application failure vs. site disaster |
| Duplicate audit trail requirements across NFR-LOG, NFR-SEC, NFR-COM | NFR Review | Single authoritative audit projection in Inventory Intelligence |
| Missing integration and bulk-import performance NFRs | NFR Review PERF-R-02 | Add architecture capacity assumptions for FR-090 go-live import |
| Tiered data architecture needed | NFR Review §8.2 | Hot/warm/cold storage strategy spanning operational, audit, and archive |

## 5. Major Architectural Risks

Risks are classified by impact on architectural integrity, delivery, and business outcomes. Mitigations are architectural — not project-management — actions.

### 5.1 Critical Risks

| Risk ID | Risk | Source | Impact | Mitigation Direction |
|---------|------|--------|--------|---------------------|
| AR-01 | **Unresolved domain hotspots block correct aggregate design** — 2 Critical (HS-001, HS-002) and 5 High hotspots open | SRS-ES-007 | Wrong persistence model, unenforceable BR-007/BR-010, failed MVP go-live | Architecture sign-off gated on Session 1 workshop outcomes; document assumptions for deferred items |
| AR-02 | **Split-brain ATP ownership** — promotional ring-fence (HS-004, P1-02) and reservation coordination (HS-007) span contexts | SRS-DM-009; SRS-ES-007 | Overselling, inconsistent availability, customer trust failure | Confirm event ownership: Commercial Campaign emits intent; Stock Position owns ATP mechanics; saga for order-reservation |
| AR-03 | **Stock Position identity fork** — lot/batch scoping undecided (HS-005, P1-05) | SRS-DM-009 | Fundamental data model divergence affecting reservation, pick, count, transfer | Adopt single Stock Position per product-location with lot child entities before detailed design |
| AR-04 | **Finance system boundary ambiguity** (HS-014) | SRS-ES-007 | Duplicate three-way match logic or missing financial controls | Early integration workshop; ERP ACL decision for MVP vs. Phase 2; IMS owns operational facts, Finance owns payment authority |
| AR-05 | **Reservation contention and partial failure** under peak load | HS-007; NFR-PERF-007 | Oversell or stale reservations; customer service incidents | Define reservation saga with compensation; prototype Class A SKU contention; reservation TTL policy (HS-016) |

### 5.2 High Risks

| Risk ID | Risk | Source | Impact | Mitigation Direction |
|---------|------|--------|--------|---------------------|
| AR-06 | **Fixed budget vs. NFR ambition** — 122 Must Have NFRs including 15-min RPO, 99.5% uptime, full security suite | BC-01; NFR Review | Over-engineering or under-delivery | MVP NFR subset (~40 requirements); phased compliance program; modular monolith to reduce ops cost |
| AR-07 | **Location freeze dual authority** (HS-003, P1-03) | SRS-DM-009 | Race conditions during physical count; unauthorized mutations | Physical Count initiates freeze; Inventory Location holds flag; Freeze Guard reads Location only |
| AR-08 | **Opening balance go-live without governing workflow** (HS-002) | SRS-ES-007 | Transactions on uncertified stock; accuracy KPI failure at launch | Opening Balance Establishment workflow; certify-before-activate chain |
| AR-09 | **Premature microservices decomposition** — 13 contexts mistaken for 13 services | SRS-DM-007 scope note | Distributed complexity exceeding ORC-04 capacity; operational failure | Context ≠ service; modular monolith first; extract only on proven need (Balance vs. Intelligence) |
| AR-10 | **Reporting load corrupting transactional performance** | SRS-DM-007 Context 13; NFR-PERF | Dock slowdown during month-end | Strict CQRS; no reporting queries against write store |
| AR-11 | **Channel integration lag causing oversell** | BRD risk register; TEC-04 | Revenue loss; customer trust damage | ACL at fulfillment boundary; manual sync interim; ATP as integration contract |
| AR-12 | **NFR internal conflicts undetected until UAT** | NFR Review | Rework, delayed go-live | Capacity model, harmonized SLA register, traceability matrix before build |

## 6. Recommended Architecture Style

### 6.1 Recommended Style

**Domain-Driven Design (DDD) with a Modular Monolith core, internal event-driven integration, and CQRS for operational analytics — evolving toward selective service extraction as scale and organizational maturity demand.**

This is a **compound architectural style**, not a single pattern. Each element addresses specific drivers:

| Style Element | Purpose | Addresses |
|---------------|---------|-----------|
| **Strategic DDD** (bounded contexts, context map, ubiquitous language) | Align software structure to business domains | AD-01–AD-07; AG-02 |
| **Modular Monolith** (context-aligned modules, single deployable unit for MVP) | Control cost and operational complexity within BC-01 and ORC-04 | AD-15, AD-16; AR-09 |
| **Hexagonal / Ports & Adapters** (per context module) | Isolate domain logic from UI, persistence, and external integrations | AD-07; AG-06 |
| **Event-Driven Architecture (internal)** | Choreograph cross-context reactions via domain events | AD-02; AG-05 |
| **CQRS** (command/query separation for Intelligence context) | Protect write-path performance from reporting load | AD-05; AR-10 |
| **Saga / Process Manager** (cross-aggregate workflows) | Coordinate reservation, transfer, and go-live with compensation | AD-04; AR-05, AR-08 |
| **Anti-Corruption Layer** (external boundaries) | Protect IMS domain from Sales/CRM and Finance/ERP models | AD-07; AR-04, AR-11 |

### 6.2 Style Justification

#### Why Domain-Driven Design

The domain analysis produced **13 bounded contexts**, **18 aggregates**, **81 domain events**, **24 domain services**, and **72 ubiquitous language terms** — indicating high domain complexity with distinct consistency boundaries. DDD is not optional decoration; it is the most direct mapping from the approved domain model to software structure.

Inventory Balance as the **core domain** warrants the richest model and protection. Supporting contexts (Catalog, Network, Governance) are upstream suppliers. Generic subdomains (Identity & Access, cross-cutting audit) may leverage commodity solutions.

#### Why Modular Monolith (Phase 1) Over Microservices

| Factor | Modular Monolith | Microservices |
|--------|------------------|---------------|
| Fixed budget (BC-01) | Single deployment, one ops pipeline | Multiplied infrastructure and monitoring cost |
| Limited IT capacity (ORC-04) | One runtime to manage | Service mesh, distributed tracing, contract versioning overhead |
| 13 contexts / phased delivery | Modules can be developed in parallel within one repo | Premature network boundaries before volume proof |
| Stock Position consistency | In-process domain events; ACID within aggregate | Distributed transaction complexity for reservation |
| NFR-AVL-001 99.5% uptime | Fewer failure domains | Cascading failure risk across services |

SRS-DM-007 explicitly states bounded contexts are **strategic design, not deployment**. The context map defines integration patterns (events, ACL, published language) that remain valid whether modules are co-located or distributed.

**Extraction candidates (Phase 2+)** if metrics justify:
- **Inventory Intelligence** — read-heavy, different scaling profile, eventual consistency acceptable
- **Identity & Access** — commodity capability, likely enterprise IdP integration
- **Integration gateway** — external Sales/CRM and Finance adapters

#### Why Internal Event-Driven Integration

Event storming revealed **12 end-to-end lifecycles** with policy chains (e.g., `PutAwayCompleted` → `StockReceived` → availability update → backorder fulfillment policy). Synchronous coupling between all contexts would violate performance drivers (AD-08) and entangle lifecycles.

Domain events provide:
- **Loose coupling** between context modules
- **Natural audit trail** feeding Inventory Intelligence
- **Extensibility** for Phase 2 policies (campaign readiness, replenishment recommendation) without modifying upstream aggregates

Events are **internal** in Phase 1 (in-process event bus or transactional outbox within the monolith). External message broker introduction is deferred until cross-system async integration volume requires it.

#### Why CQRS for Inventory Intelligence

Inventory Intelligence owns **no write aggregates** — only projections (movement history, audit trail, KPIs, alerts, valuation snapshots). Mixing these queries into Stock Position or Order Fulfillment is the "reporting database inside the transaction" anti-pattern identified in SRS-DM-007.

CQRS enables:
- Optimized read models for dashboards (NFR-PERF-004, NFR-PERF-023)
- 7-year audit retention without bloating operational tables (NFR-COM-019, NFR-COM-020)
- Rebuild projections from event history after corruption or schema evolution

#### Why Saga Pattern for Cross-Aggregate Workflows

Single-aggregate ACID is sufficient **within** Stock Position, Goods Receipt, or Customer Order. Cross-context workflows — confirm order then reserve stock, dispatch transfer then deduct source and increase destination, certify opening balance then activate location — require **long-running coordination with compensation**.

Event storming hotspot HS-007 (reservation coordination) and policies POL-001/002 explicitly demand a documented saga: success path and failure compensation must be architectural first-class concerns, not implementation afterthoughts.

### 6.4 Phased Architecture Evolution

| Phase | Period | Architectural Focus |
|-------|--------|---------------------|
| **Phase 1 — Stabilize** | Months 0–6 | Modular monolith with core contexts: Catalog, Network, Balance, Inbound, Fulfillment, Accuracy (cycle count), Governance, Identity, Intelligence (basic projections). Internal events. Single-location then sequential rollout. |
| **Phase 2 — Perform** | Months 6–12 | Full Procurement, Network Transfer, Returns, Commercial Campaign modules. Enhanced sagas (backorder priority, transfer-before-buy). Evaluate Intelligence read-tier scaling. External integration hardening. |
| **Phase 3 — Decide** | Months 12–18 | Finance ACL and valuation snapshots. Advanced KPI and network analytics. Selective extraction if volume metrics warrant. Tiered data architecture fully operational. |

### 6.5 Alternatives Considered and Rejected

| Alternative | Reason for Rejection |
|-------------|---------------------|
| **Traditional layered monolith (no domain modules)** | Cannot preserve 13 context boundaries; high coupling risk; violates AG-02 |
| **Microservices from day one** | Disproportionate ops cost under BC-01/ORC-04; distributed consistency risk for Stock Position (AR-09) |
| **CRUD-centric data model** | Cannot express 32 business rules, SoD, and event choreography; leads to anemic validation scattered in UI |
| **Single shared database schema without context ownership** | Encourages cross-context joins and dual ATP writers; contradicts SRS-DM-007 integration patterns |
| **Offline-first / sync architecture** | Explicitly out of scope (TEC-03); adds conflict resolution complexity without MVP requirement |

### 6.6 Architecture Decision Records (Preview)

The following decisions will be formalized as ADRs in subsequent architecture documents:

| ADR Topic | Decision Direction |
|-----------|-------------------|
| ADR-001 Deployment topology | Modular monolith for Phase 1 |
| ADR-002 Cross-context integration | Domain events with transactional outbox |
| ADR-003 Read/write separation | CQRS for Inventory Intelligence |
| ADR-004 Stock Position identity | Single aggregate per product-location (pending HS-005 confirmation) |
| ADR-005 Reservation coordination | Saga with defined compensation (pending HS-007 workshop) |
| ADR-006 External finance boundary | ACL with IMS as operational SoR (pending HS-014 workshop) |
| ADR-007 Authentication | Enterprise SSO with location-scoped RBAC |
| ADR-008 Data retention tiers | Hot / warm / cold aligned to NFR-COM-019 |

---

## 7. Architecture Vision Summary

The Inventory Management System will be built as a **domain-driven, modular platform** centered on **Inventory Balance** as the authoritative quantity core. Cross-context collaboration will follow **event-driven choreography** and **explicit sagas** where business workflows span aggregates. Operational analytics and compliance evidence will flow through a **CQRS read side** (Inventory Intelligence), protecting transactional integrity and performance.

Architecture prioritizes **governed correctness, auditability, and phased credible control** over premature distribution. The modular monolith approach honors the **fixed budget and limited IT capacity** while preserving **decomposition readiness** as the organization scales locations, channels, and transaction volume toward the 3–5 year vision.

**Gate to proceed to Solution Architecture:** Resolution of Critical hotspots (HS-001, HS-002), confirmation of Stock Position identity model (HS-005), and documented integration contracts for freeze authority (HS-003) and reservation coordination (HS-007).

### Purpose

This document defines the **System Context** for the Inventory Management System (IMS) — the single boundary within which inventory truth is established, governed, and consumed. It identifies who and what interacts with IMS, what data crosses each boundary, and why each interaction exists.

### System Purpose (Context Summary)

The IMS is the organization's **inventory system of record** — authoritative for stock quantities, movements, reservations, replenishment state, and inventory audit evidence. It is **not** the enterprise system of record for sales, finance, HR, or channel commerce (BRD §8.2; TEC-01).

---

## 1. Primary Users

IMS serves **19 business user roles** (BRD §11). External trading partners do **not** hold standing IMS accounts in MVP scope. Users access IMS via standard web browser on company-approved devices (TEC-03, TEC-06).

### 1.1 User Groups

| Group | User Roles | Primary Purpose |
|-------|------------|-----------------|
| **Operations & Warehouse** | Inventory Controller, Receiving Clerk, Warehouse Staff, Picker/Packer, Warehouse Manager, Regional/Store Manager, Operations Director | Record and control physical inventory — receive, store, count, transfer, pick, ship, quarantine |
| **Supply & Procurement** | Buyer, Purchasing Manager | Authorize inbound supply — requisitions, purchase orders, inbound planning, replenishment response |
| **Commercial & Customer-Facing** | Sales Representative, Customer Service Representative, Marketing Manager | Confirm availability, reserve and fulfill orders, manage returns, ring-fence promotional stock |
| **Finance & Governance** | Finance Manager, Internal Auditor, External Auditor *(temporary)* | Reconcile valuation, three-way match, audit trail review, control testing |
| **Executive Oversight** | CEO, CFO | Review inventory KPIs, valuation alignment, strategic performance |
| **Technology Administration** | System Administrator | Provision users, assign location-scoped roles, enforce SoD at access layer |

### 1.2 Primary User Detail

| ID | Role | Key Interactions With IMS |
|----|------|---------------------------|
| UR-01 | Inventory Controller | Product/location master, policies, counts, opening balances, governance |
| UR-02 | Receiving Clerk | Goods receipt verification, discrepancies, return receipt |
| UR-03 | Warehouse Staff | Put-away, cycle count, transfer dispatch/receipt |
| UR-04 | Picker/Packer | Pick verification, shipment dispatch |
| UR-05 | Warehouse Manager | Approvals, quarantine, adjustments, exceptions, returns disposition |
| UR-06 | Regional/Store Manager | Transfer requests, local stock monitoring |
| UR-07 | Operations Director | Transfer/adjustment approval, network rebalancing, executive operations view |
| UR-08 | Buyer | Purchase orders, inbound scheduling, replenishment execution |
| UR-09 | Purchasing Manager | Requisition approval, low-stock response |
| UR-10 | Sales Representative | ATP inquiry, order availability confirmation |
| UR-11 | Customer Service Representative | Order confirm/cancel, reservation, backorder, RMA, fulfillment status |
| UR-12 | Marketing Manager | Promotional stock allocation, campaign readiness |
| UR-13 | Finance Manager | Supplier invoice, three-way match, valuation snapshot, GL reconciliation |
| UR-14 | Internal Auditor | Read-only audit trail, movement history, SoD evidence |
| UR-15 | External Auditor | Temporary read-only access during statutory audit |
| UR-16 | CEO / CFO | Executive dashboards and KPI reports |
| UR-17 | System Administrator | User accounts, role assignments, location scope |

---

## 2. External Systems

External systems are organization or partner systems **outside the IMS boundary** that exchange business facts or receive inventory-derived information. Integration depth varies by phase (TEC-04, TEC-05).

| ID | External System | MVP Integration | Phase |
|----|-----------------|-----------------|-------|
| EXT-01 | **Sales / Order Management (CRM)** | Manual or batch order intake; CS/Sales enter fulfillment commands | MVP: indirect; Phase 2+: API/ACL |
| EXT-02 | **Finance ERP / General Ledger** | Scheduled export; manual reconciliation (TEC-05) | MVP: manual; Phase 3: automated ACL |
| EXT-03 | **Sales Channel / E-Commerce / Marketplace** | No real-time feed (TEC-04); manual stock updates | Phase 2+ |
| EXT-04 | **Supplier / Vendor** | PO communicated outside IMS; physical delivery triggers receipt | MVP: human-mediated |
| EXT-05 | **Logistics / Carrier Partner** | Tracking and delay info via operational workflow | MVP: human-mediated |
| EXT-06 | **Customer (B2B / B2C)** | No direct IMS access; interacts via sales channels and CS | External participant |
| EXT-07 | **Marketing / Campaign Planning** | Campaign plans may originate externally; IMS holds ring-fence | Phase 2 |
| EXT-08 | **HR / Enterprise Directory** | User identity source for provisioning | MVP: manual or sync |
| EXT-09 | **Customs / Regulatory Authority** | Clearance decisions affect quarantine release | Phase 2 if bonded in scope |

*Trading partners (EXT-04, EXT-05, EXT-06) do not execute commands inside IMS — internal actors record outcomes.*

---

## 3. Third-Party Services

Third-party services are **managed capabilities** consumed by IMS infrastructure. They are not business participants but enable security, notification, resilience, and operations.

| ID | Third-Party Service | Purpose | MVP |
|----|---------------------|---------|-----|
| SVC-01 | **Enterprise Identity Provider (SSO / Directory)** | Authenticate users; optional federated identity (LDAP/Entra ID/Okta) | Should Have |
| SVC-02 | **Email / Notification Gateway** | Deliver low-stock alerts, approval requests, exception escalations (NFR-PERF-014) | Must Have |
| SVC-03 | **SMS Gateway** *(optional)* | Urgent operational alerts for warehouse supervisors | Could Have |
| SVC-04 | **Cloud Hosting Platform** | Run IMS application and data services | Must Have |
| SVC-05 | **Backup & Disaster Recovery Service** | Protect stock balances, transactions, audit logs; ≤15-min RPO (NFR-BDR-001) | Must Have |
| SVC-06 | **Monitoring & Alerting Platform** | Availability, performance, error, and KPI monitoring (NFR-MON) | Must Have |
| SVC-07 | **Certificate / Secrets Management** | TLS, API keys, credential rotation | Must Have |
| SVC-08 | **Time Synchronization (NTP)** | Consistent timestamps for audit trail and movement ordering | Must Have |

*Excluded from business context (infrastructure only): report rendering engine, internal job scheduler — treated as IMS internal components.*

---

## 4. Data Exchanged & Communication Purpose

### 4.1 User ↔ IMS

| User Group | Data Sent to IMS | Data Received From IMS | Communication Purpose |
|------------|------------------|------------------------|----------------------|
| Operations & Warehouse | Receipt lines, put-away confirmations, count results, transfer dispatch/receipt, pick/ship confirmations, quarantine actions, adjustments | Stock positions, ATP, location status, freeze alerts, pick lists, transfer authorizations, operational alerts | Execute and control physical inventory with governed accuracy |
| Supply & Procurement | Requisitions, POs, inbound schedules, delay notices | Low-stock alerts, network ATP, inbound pipeline status, replenishment recommendations | Commit and track inbound supply |
| Commercial | Availability checks, order confirm/cancel, reservations, backorders, RMAs, promotional allocations | ATP by SKU/location, reservation status, shipment status, backorder pipeline, campaign readiness | Sell and fulfill without overselling |
| Finance & Governance | Supplier invoices, match decisions, valuation reconciliation inputs | Movement history, receipt facts, match results, valuation snapshots, write-off records, audit exports | Financial control and statutory audit |
| Executive | Report filters, dashboard scope | KPIs — fill rate, accuracy, turnover, stockout, valuation variance | Strategic oversight |
| System Administrator | User profiles, role assignments, location scope | SoD violation alerts, access audit log | Secure, scoped access |

### 4.2 External System ↔ IMS

| External System | Direction | Data Exchanged | Communication Purpose |
|-----------------|-----------|----------------|----------------------|
| **Sales / Order Management** | → IMS | Order header, line items (SKU, qty), ship-from preference, customer ref | Initiate availability check and reservation |
| | ← IMS | ATP confirmation, reservation ID, fulfillment status, shipment notice | Prevent oversell; synchronize order execution state |
| **Finance ERP / GL** | → IMS | GL inventory balance, cost method parameters, period status | Month-end reconciliation |
| | ← IMS | Valuation snapshot, adjustment/write-off facts, three-way match outcome, consignment transfer events | Align operational and financial inventory records |
| **Sales Channel / E-Commerce** | ← IMS *(Phase 2+)* | ATP or available qty feed by SKU/channel | Reduce channel oversell (TEC-04 risk mitigation) |
| **Supplier / Vendor** | → IMS *(via clerk)* | ASN/delivery notice, invoice, discrepancy response | Trigger receipt verification and invoice match |
| | ← IMS *(via buyer)* | PO, PO change/cancel, discrepancy claim | Commercial commitment and claims |
| **Logistics / Carrier** | → IMS *(via staff)* | Pickup confirmation, delivery proof, delay reason | Complete shipment/transfer; record in-transit delays |
| | ← IMS *(via staff)* | Shipment/transfer dispatch notice | Coordinate pickup |
| **Customer** | → IMS *(via CS/channel)* | Order, cancellation, backorder ack, return request | Demand and reverse logistics intake |
| | ← IMS *(via CS/channel)* | Availability answer, shipment tracking, RMA, backorder notice | Customer commitment and service |
| **Marketing / Campaign** | → IMS | Campaign SKU list, qty, channel, period | Ring-fence stock for promotional readiness |
| | ← IMS | Allocation status, readiness gap alerts | Campaign launch confidence |
| **HR / Directory** | → IMS | Employee ID, name, department, status | Provision/deprovision user accounts |
| **Customs / Regulatory** | → IMS *(via compliance)* | Clearance grant, hold notice, recall directive | Release or hold bonded/quarantined stock |
| **External Auditor** | ← IMS | Audit trail export, movement history, count certification, SoD evidence | Independent control testing |

### 4.3 Third-Party Service ↔ IMS

| Service | Data Exchanged | Communication Purpose |
|---------|----------------|----------------------|
| Identity Provider | Auth tokens, user claims, group membership | Single sign-on; unique user attribution (NFR-SEC-001) |
| Email / SMS Gateway | Alert payloads, recipient, delivery status | Timely operational notification (NFR-PERF-014) |
| Cloud Platform | Compute, storage, network | Host application and data |
| Backup / DR | Database snapshots, transaction logs, config | Business continuity; ≤15-min RPO (NFR-BDR-001) |
| Monitoring | Metrics, logs, traces, alert events | Detect outage within 5 min (NFR-MON-001) |

```
    ┌──────┴──────┐      ┌──────┴──────┐      ┌──────┴──────┐
    │  Supplier   │      │  Logistics  │      │  Customs /  │
    │  / Vendor   │      │  / Carrier  │      │ Regulatory  │
    └─────────────┘      └─────────────┘      └─────────────┘
      goods, invoices      shipments, delays     clearance, holds
      (via receiving)      (via warehouse)       (via compliance)

    ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
    THIRD-PARTY (infrastructure): SSO · Email · Cloud · Backup · Monitoring
    ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
```

### 5.3 Interaction Legend

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| `───►` | Primary data or command flow |
| `◄───` | Response, query result, or outbound notification |
| `(Phase 2+)` | Not in MVP integration scope per TEC-04 / TEC-05 |
| `via clerk/staff` | Human-mediated — no direct system integration in MVP |

---

## 6. System Boundary Rules

| Rule | Statement |
|------|-----------|
| **SB-01** | IMS owns inventory quantity state, movement history, and inventory audit evidence |
| **SB-02** | IMS does **not** own general ledger, customer master, pricing, or sales pipeline |
| **SB-03** | Customer orders may **originate** in Sales/Order Management; IMS owns **fulfillment-relevant subset** via ACL |
| **SB-04** | Finance ERP remains **financial system of record**; IMS publishes operational valuation facts |
| **SB-05** | External trading partners interact through **business workflows**, not standing IMS accounts (MVP) |
| **SB-06** | Notifications are **delivered** via third-party gateways; alert **content and routing** are IMS responsibility |
| **SB-07** | Channel ATP sync is **out of MVP scope** (TEC-04); oversell risk managed by manual process until Phase 2 |

---

## 7. Phase Integration Summary

| Integration | MVP (Months 0–6) | Phase 2 (6–12) | Phase 3 (12–18) |
|-------------|------------------|----------------|-----------------|
| Sales / Order Management | Manual entry / batch import | API with ACL | Bi-directional status sync |
| Finance ERP | Export + manual reconcile (TEC-05) | Scheduled file / API | Automated valuation alignment |
| Sales Channel | Manual stock updates | ATP feed | Real-time availability |
| Supplier | Human workflow | Optional ASN import | Supplier portal (long-term) |
| Marketing Campaign | In-app only | External campaign feed ACL | — |
| HR Directory | Manual provisioning | Directory sync | Federated SSO |

# Architecture Style Recommendation
## Inventory Management System

---

## Document Information

| Attribute | Detail |
|-----------|--------|
| **Document ID** | SRS-SA-002 |
| **Document Title** | Architecture Style Recommendation — Inventory Management System |
| **Version** | 1.0 |
| **Status** | Draft |
| **Document Owner** | Solution Architect |
| **Prepared For** | Steering committee, product owner, delivery leads, and technical architects |
| **Date** | July 6, 2026 |
| **Classification** | Internal — Architecture Confidential |
| **Scope** | Architecture style evaluation and recommendation — no technology stack, module design, or implementation detail |

### Related Documents

| Document | ID | Relationship |
|----------|-----|--------------|
| Architecture Vision | SRS-SA-001 | Parent strategic direction |
| Bounded Contexts | SRS-DM-007 | Domain decomposition input |
| Domain Model Review | SRS-DM-009 | Core domain and gate findings |
| Business Requirements Document | BRD-IMS-001 | Constraints, objectives, phased scope |
| Non-Functional Requirements Suite | 204 NFRs | Quality attribute drivers |

### Document Purpose

This document evaluates six candidate architecture styles against the Inventory Management System's business drivers, domain complexity, non-functional requirements, and delivery constraints. It provides a structured comparison and a final recommendation to guide solution architecture and implementation planning.

---

## 1. Evaluation Context

### 1.1 Project Characteristics Relevant to Style Selection

| Characteristic | Detail | Style Implication |
|----------------|--------|-------------------|
| **Domain complexity** | 13 bounded contexts, 18 aggregates, 81 domain events, 32 business rules | Favors domain-centric styles over purely technical layering |
| **Core domain** | Inventory Balance (Stock Position, ATP, reservations) — high write contention | Requires strong consistency within core; careful cross-boundary integration |
| **Integration pattern** | Event-driven choreography, sagas, ACLs to Sales/CRM and Finance/ERP | Needs ports/adapters and explicit boundary protection |
| **Read/write profile** | Transactional operations + heavy reporting/audit (Inventory Intelligence) | CQRS-friendly; reporting must not burden write path |
| **Delivery horizon** | 18-month phased initiative; MVP in Months 0–6 | Style must support incremental delivery, not big-bang |
| **Budget** | Fixed initiative budget (BC-01) | Limits operational overhead of distributed architectures |
| **IT capacity** | Limited internal IT operations (ORC-04) | Fewer deployable units and simpler runtime preferred for MVP |
| **Scale trajectory** | 15% near-term / 30% medium-term growth; multi-location rollout | Style must scale without forced rewrite |
| **Quality priorities** | Data integrity, security/compliance, availability (99.5%), auditability | Governance and traceability are non-negotiable |

### 1.2 Evaluation Criteria

Each architecture style is assessed against:

| Criterion | Weight | Description |
|-----------|--------|-------------|
| **Domain alignment** | High | Supports 13 bounded contexts and DDD strategic design |
| **Correctness & integrity** | High | Protects ATP invariants, SoD, and audit trail |
| **MVP feasibility** | High | Deliverable within Months 0–6 under BC-01 and ORC-04 |
| **Operational simplicity** | High | Runnable and maintainable by limited IT capacity |
| **Evolvability** | Medium | Supports Phase 2–3 without architectural replacement |
| **Performance fit** | Medium | Meets sub-2s ATP and sub-3s operational response targets |
| **Team scalability** | Medium | Aligns with squad/team structure as delivery grows |
| **Testability** | Medium | Enables isolated testing of domain rules and integrations |

### 1.3 Important Distinction — Deployment Style vs. Internal Structure

Several options in this comparison operate at **different levels of abstraction**:

| Level | Styles |
|-------|--------|
| **Deployment / system topology** | Modular Monolith, Microservices |
| **Internal code organization** | Layered, Clean, Hexagonal, Onion |

These are **not always mutually exclusive**. A modular monolith can implement hexagonal or clean architecture inside each module. The final recommendation combines styles at the appropriate level rather than selecting a single label.

---

## 2. Architecture Style Comparison

### 2.1 Layered Architecture

**Description:** Organizes the system into horizontal tiers — typically Presentation → Application/Business Logic → Data Access → Database — with dependencies flowing downward.

#### Advantages

| Advantage | Benefit for IMS |
|-----------|-----------------|
| Familiar and widely understood | Low learning curve for mixed-skill delivery teams |
| Clear separation of UI, logic, and persistence | Straightforward CRUD screens for master data (products, locations) |
| Simple deployment model | Single application unit aligns with budget constraints |
| Easy to bootstrap | Fast initial scaffolding for MVP timelines |
| Tooling support | Most frameworks default to layered structure |

#### Disadvantages

| Disadvantage | Risk for IMS |
|--------------|--------------|
| **Domain logic leaks across layers** | 32 business rules and SoD policies scatter into services, controllers, and repositories |
| **No natural bounded context boundaries** | 13 contexts collapse into shared services and tables |
| **Database-centric design tendency** | Stock Position invariants driven by schema rather than aggregate behavior |
| **High coupling over time** | Cross-cutting changes (e.g., ATP formula, freeze rules) ripple through all layers |
| **Reporting couples to transactional path** | Dashboard queries against same tables degrade dock performance (AR-10) |
| **Poor fit for event-driven coordination** | 81 domain events have no first-class home; added as afterthought |

#### Suitability for This Project

| Dimension | Rating | Rationale |
|-----------|--------|-----------|
| Domain alignment | **Low** | Cannot express 13 bounded contexts or Inventory Balance as core domain |
| MVP feasibility | **High** | Fast to start, but accrues rework as rules accumulate |
| Long-term evolvability | **Low** | Becomes monolithic "big ball of mud" under cross-location growth |
| NFR compliance | **Medium** | Achievable with discipline, but audit and CQRS require bolt-on patterns |

**Overall suitability: Low** — acceptable only for trivial CRUD subsets, not as the system-wide style.

#### Selected or Rejected?

**Rejected as the primary architecture style.**

Layered architecture does not provide the domain boundaries, event transparency, or integration isolation that the approved domain model requires. It may be used **locally within a module's infrastructure slice** (e.g., repository implementations beneath domain core) but must not define the system's top-level structure.

---

### 2.2 Clean Architecture

**Description:** Robert Martin's concentric dependency rule — entities at the center, use cases around them, interface adapters outside, frameworks at the edge. Dependencies point inward; business rules are independent of UI, database, and external systems.

#### Advantages

| Advantage | Benefit for IMS |
|-----------|-----------------|
| **Domain-centric dependency rule** | Stock Position, Goods Receipt, and Order aggregates stay free of framework code |
| **Testable use cases** | Command handlers for ReserveStock, ReceiveGoods testable without database |
| **Framework independence** | UI swap (web → mobile warehouse) without touching domain rules |
| **Explicit use case layer** | Maps cleanly to 48 use cases and application services |
| **Supports ports and adapters** | Natural fit for ACL to Sales/CRM and Finance/ERP |

#### Disadvantages

| Disadvantage | Risk for IMS |
|--------------|--------------|
| **Ceremony and boilerplate** | Many interfaces and DTO mappings across 13 contexts |
| **No deployment guidance** | Clean Architecture is internal structure only — does not resolve monolith vs. microservices |
| **No modular boundary enforcement** | Teams can still create cross-context imports without compile-time module boundaries |
| **Learning curve** | Requires discipline to avoid "clean in name only" anemic entities |
| **Event-driven patterns not prescribed** | Domain events and CQRS must be added explicitly |

#### Suitability for This Project

| Dimension | Rating | Rationale |
|-----------|--------|-----------|
| Domain alignment | **High** | Aligns with DDD aggregates and domain services |
| MVP feasibility | **Medium–High** | Achievable with templates; overhead manageable per module |
| Long-term evolvability | **High** | Use cases and entities stable as infrastructure changes |
| NFR compliance | **High** | Supports testability, ACL, and separation of concerns |

**Overall suitability: High** — as **internal structure within each bounded context module**.

#### Selected or Rejected?

**Selected as an internal organizing principle** (per bounded context module), **not as the sole architecture label**.

Clean Architecture provides the dependency discipline needed to protect domain rules (BR-001, BR-002, BR-005, SoD) from infrastructure concerns. It does not address cross-module integration, deployment topology, or CQRS — those require complementary patterns.

---

### 2.3 Hexagonal Architecture (Ports and Adapters)

**Description:** Alistair Cockburn's model placing the application core at the center with **ports** (interfaces) and **adapters** (implementations) for driving actors (UI, API) and driven actors (database, external systems, message bus).

#### Advantages

| Advantage | Benefit for IMS |
|-----------|-----------------|
| **Explicit integration boundaries** | ACL for Sales/CRM orders and Finance/ERP valuation as outbound adapters |
| **Multiple driving adapters** | Web office UI, warehouse mobile, and integration API share same core ports |
| **Swappable infrastructure** | Change persistence or messaging without altering Stock Position logic |
| **Natural anti-corruption layers** | External order model translated at adapter, not in domain |
| **Testability via port mocks** | Simulate ERP responses for three-way match scenarios |
| **Aligns with event storming** | Commands enter via driving ports; events exit via driven ports |

#### Disadvantages

| Disadvantage | Risk for IMS |
|--------------|--------------|
| **Adapter proliferation** | 13 contexts × multiple adapters (DB, events, external) increases surface area |
| **Mapping overhead** | DTO ↔ domain object translation at every boundary |
| **No strategic domain map** | Hexagonal is tactical — does not define bounded context relationships |
| **Risk of anemic ports** | Ports become CRUD pass-throughs if domain model is weak |
| **Distributed hexagons = microservices** | Without modular monolith discipline, each hexagon drifts to separate service |

#### Suitability for This Project

| Dimension | Rating | Rationale |
|-----------|--------|-----------|
| Domain alignment | **High** | Protects core domain from external system models (HS-014) |
| MVP feasibility | **High** | Adapters can start simple (in-process) and evolve |
| Long-term evolvability | **High** | External integrations change frequently; adapters absorb change |
| NFR compliance | **High** | Supports security (auth adapter), logging (observability adapter), ERP ACL |

**Overall suitability: High** — especially for **Inventory Balance**, **Order Fulfillment**, and **Inbound Receiving** contexts with external touchpoints.

#### Selected or Rejected?

**Selected as the integration and isolation pattern** within each bounded context module.

Hexagonal architecture is the primary mechanism for implementing AG-06 (integration-ready enterprise capability) and mitigating AR-04 (finance boundary) and AR-11 (channel integration). It complements Clean/Onion rather than replacing them.

---

### 2.4 Onion Architecture

**Description:** Jeffrey Palermo's variant of layered architecture with the domain model at the center, domain services surrounding it, application services outside, and infrastructure on the outermost ring. Like Clean Architecture, dependencies point inward.

#### Advantages

| Advantage | Benefit for IMS |
|-----------|-----------------|
| **Domain model at the center** | Reinforces Inventory Balance as core with rich entity behavior |
| **Clear ring boundaries** | Domain → Application → Infrastructure progression is teachable |
| **Repository interfaces in domain ring** | Persistence abstraction without ORM leaking into aggregates |
| **Consistent with DDD** | Aggregates, domain services, and repositories have natural homes |
| **Incremental adoption** | Teams can onion-wrap one context at a time during phased delivery |

#### Disadvantages

| Disadvantage | Risk for IMS |
|--------------|--------------|
| **Substantial overlap with Clean Architecture** | Teams may debate nomenclature (use case vs. application service) without design benefit |
| **No cross-context guidance** | 13 onions in one codebase need modular monolith rules to prevent coupling |
| **Application service bloat risk** | Complex sagas (reservation coordination) can inflate the application ring |
| **Event publishing not explicit** | Domain events need deliberate placement — domain ring or application ring |
| **Shared infrastructure temptation** | Shared outer-ring components (logging, auth) can create hidden coupling |

#### Suitability for This Project

| Dimension | Rating | Rationale |
|-----------|--------|-----------|
| Domain alignment | **High** | Supports rich Stock Position aggregate with invariants |
| MVP feasibility | **Medium–High** | Similar effort to Clean Architecture |
| Long-term evolvability | **High** | Infrastructure rings swappable per context |
| NFR compliance | **High** | Domain-centric testing supports rule verification |

**Overall suitability: High** — largely **equivalent to Clean Architecture** for IMS purposes.

#### Selected or Rejected?

**Selected in principle, merged with Clean Architecture** — use one consistent internal ring model across all context modules to avoid team confusion.

Onion and Clean Architecture solve the same problem. The IMS architecture standard will use **"Clean/Hexagonal"** as the documented term: domain core (entities, aggregates, domain services) → application layer (commands, queries, sagas) → adapters (persistence, messaging, external systems).

---

### 2.5 Modular Monolith

**Description:** A single deployable application composed of **loosely coupled modules** aligned to domain boundaries (bounded contexts). Modules communicate through well-defined interfaces or domain events — not shared database tables or direct internal API calls across boundaries.

#### Advantages

| Advantage | Benefit for IMS |
|-----------|-----------------|
| **Single deployment unit** | One runtime, one pipeline — fits BC-01 fixed budget and ORC-04 limited ops |
| **Bounded context alignment** | 13 modules map to SRS-DM-007 without network overhead |
| **ACID within module** | Stock Position aggregate transactions remain in-process and strongly consistent |
| **In-process domain events** | 81 events published via internal bus or transactional outbox — no broker required for MVP |
| **Phased module activation** | Enable Procurement, Transfer, Campaign modules in Phase 2 without new deployments |
| **Simpler NFR achievement** | 99.5% uptime easier with fewer failure domains than microservices |
| **Decomposition readiness** | Modules with clear interfaces can be extracted to services later (Intelligence, Identity) |
| **Faster cross-module refactoring** | Compiler enforces module boundaries; rename/extract safer than distributed refactor |

#### Disadvantages

| Disadvantage | Risk for IMS |
|--------------|--------------|
| **Requires discipline** | Without enforced module boundaries, devolves to traditional monolith |
| **Scaling limitations** | Cannot independently scale Stock Position writes vs. reporting reads without read-side separation |
| **Shared runtime blast radius** | Defect in one module can affect entire application availability |
| **Technology homogeneity** | All modules share same language, framework, and database stack |
| **Team coordination at scale** | Large teams on one codebase need strong ownership rules to avoid merge conflicts |
| **Not a complete architecture** | Still needs internal structure (Clean/Hexagonal) and integration patterns (events, CQRS) |

#### Suitability for This Project

| Dimension | Rating | Rationale |
|-----------|--------|-----------|
| Domain alignment | **High** | Direct mapping to 13 bounded contexts |
| MVP feasibility | **High** | Fastest path to credible control by Month 6 |
| Long-term evolvability | **High** | Extraction path for Intelligence and integration gateway |
| NFR compliance | **High** | Meets availability, performance, and budget constraints |
| Operational simplicity | **High** | Best fit for limited IT capacity |

**Overall suitability: Very High** — strongest **deployment topology** choice for Phase 1–2.

#### Selected or Rejected?

**Selected as the primary deployment and system topology style for Phase 1 and Phase 2.**

Modular monolith is the only deployment style that simultaneously satisfies fixed budget, limited IT capacity, strong Stock Position consistency, phased delivery, and the strategic domain decomposition already approved. SRS-DM-007 explicitly states bounded contexts are strategic design — not microservice boundaries.

---

### 2.6 Microservices

**Description:** Decomposes the system into **independently deployable services**, each owning its data, communicating via network protocols (REST, gRPC, messaging). Often aligned to bounded contexts — one service per context.

#### Advantages

| Advantage | Benefit for IMS |
|-----------|-----------------|
| **Independent scaling** | Scale Order Fulfillment and Inventory Balance separately under peak load |
| **Technology heterogeneity** | Different stacks per service (e.g., analytics service in specialized engine) |
| **Team autonomy** | Each squad owns full service lifecycle — deploy without coordinating other teams |
| **Fault isolation** | Reporting service failure does not take down receiving dock |
| **Bounded context mapping** | Natural 1:1 with 13 contexts — attractive on paper |
| **Clear data ownership** | Each service owns its database — no shared tables |

#### Disadvantages

| Disadvantage | Risk for IMS |
|--------------|--------------|
| **Distributed consistency complexity** | Reservation saga (HS-007) across Order and Balance services requires eventual consistency, compensation, and idempotency — high defect risk |
| **Operational overhead** | Service mesh, distributed tracing, contract testing, multiple CI/CD pipelines — exceeds ORC-04 capacity |
| **Infrastructure cost** | Multiple runtimes, databases, brokers strain BC-01 fixed budget |
| **Latency on hot paths** | ATP lookup and reservation cross service boundaries — threatens NFR-PERF-002 (2s) |
| **Premature decomposition risk** | 16 open domain hotspots (SRS-ES-007) make service boundaries unstable before implementation |
| **Cross-service transactions** | Put-away → stock available → backorder fulfill chain becomes fragile distributed workflow |
| **Integration testing burden** | End-to-end tests require full service topology — slows MVP delivery |
| **Data duplication and sync** | Product SKU and Location Code replicated across services or queried synchronously |

#### Suitability for This Project

| Dimension | Rating | Rationale |
|-----------|--------|-----------|
| Domain alignment | **Medium** (theoretical) / **Low** (practical) | Contexts are clear, but hotspots and sagas make boundaries premature |
| MVP feasibility | **Low** | Months 0–6 delivery at risk from distributed complexity |
| Long-term evolvability | **High** (at maturity) | Valid at 3–5 year scale with mature ops — not at initiative start |
| NFR compliance | **Medium** | Achievable but expensive; 99.5% uptime harder across many services |
| Operational simplicity | **Very Low** | Conflicts directly with ORC-04 |

**Overall suitability: Low for Phase 1–2; Medium for selective Phase 3 extraction.**

#### Selected or Rejected?

**Rejected as the initial system topology. Approved as a future evolution path for proven extraction candidates.**

Microservices address scale and team autonomy problems the organization does not yet have at MVP. The risk of distributed data inconsistency on Stock Position — the system's core value — outweighs theoretical benefits. Selective extraction of **Inventory Intelligence** (read-only, CQRS) and **integration gateway** may be reconsidered in Phase 3 when volume metrics and ops maturity justify the cost.

---

---

## 4. Final Recommendation

### 4.1 Recommended Architecture Style

**Modular Monolith with Clean/Hexagonal internal architecture, domain-driven bounded context modules, internal event-driven integration, and CQRS for Inventory Intelligence.**

This is a **deliberate composition** of complementary styles at the correct abstraction level:

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  DEPLOYMENT LAYER          Modular Monolith (single deployable unit)  │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  MODULE LAYER              13 Bounded Context Modules                   │
│                            (compile-time or package-enforced boundaries) │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  INTERNAL STRUCTURE        Clean / Onion rings per module:              │
│                            Domain → Application → Adapters               │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  INTEGRATION PATTERN       Hexagonal ports/adapters:                    │
│                            - Driving: Web, Mobile, API                    │
│                            - Driven: DB, Event Bus, ERP, CRM             │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  CROSS-MODULE COORDINATION Internal domain events + sagas               │
│                            (transactional outbox within monolith)        │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  READ MODEL SEPARATION     CQRS — Inventory Intelligence projections    │
│                            (extractable to separate service in Phase 3)  │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

### 4.2 Why This Combination Wins

| Project Requirement | How the Recommended Style Delivers |
|---------------------|-----------------------------------|
| Single source of inventory truth (BO-01) | Inventory Balance module owns Stock Position; other modules interact via commands and events — no shared mutable state |
| 13 bounded contexts (SRS-DM-007) | One module per context with published integration contracts |
| 32 business rules + SoD (BR-001 – BR-032) | Clean/Hexagonal domain core enforces invariants; governance consulted via ports |
| 81 domain events (SRS-ES-001) | Internal event bus with transactional outbox ensures reliable cross-module reactions |
| Sub-2s ATP lookup (NFR-PERF-002) | In-process reads and optimized query side; no cross-service network hops in hot path |
| 99.5% uptime (NFR-AVL-001) | Single runtime reduces failure domains vs. microservices |
| Fixed budget (BC-01) | One deployment pipeline, one operational surface |
| Limited IT capacity (ORC-04) | No service mesh, no multi-broker ops for MVP |
| Phased delivery (Months 0–18) | Modules activated per phase; Phase 2 contexts added without topology change |
| Finance/CRM integration (HS-014) | Hexagonal ACL adapters at module boundary |
| Reporting without dock slowdown (AR-10) | CQRS projections in Intelligence module, separate read store |
| Future scale (NFR-SCAL-001) | Intelligence and integration gateway extractable when proven necessary |

### 4.3 What We Explicitly Avoid

| Anti-Pattern | Why |
|--------------|-----|
| **Layered monolith** (UI → Service → Repository → DB for entire system) | Collapses 13 contexts; rules scatter; no event-first design |
| **Microservices day one** (13 services) | Distributed consistency risk on ATP; ops cost exceeds constraints |
| **Clean Architecture without modules** | Dependency rule alone does not prevent cross-context coupling |
| **Modular monolith without events** | Cross-context workflows become synchronous spaghetti across modules |
| **Shared database tables across modules** | Violates context ownership; enables bypass of Stock Position invariants |

### 4.4 Phased Style Evolution

| Phase | Period | Architecture Emphasis |
|-------|--------|----------------------|
| **Phase 1** | Months 0–6 | Modular monolith; core modules (Balance, Inbound, Fulfillment, Catalog, Network, Governance, Identity); basic Intelligence projections; in-process events |
| **Phase 2** | Months 6–12 | Add Procurement, Transfer, Returns, Campaign modules; formalize sagas; strengthen event catalog; evaluate read-store scaling |
| **Phase 3** | Months 12–18 | Finance ACL hardening; advanced Intelligence; **evaluate extraction** of Intelligence read service and integration gateway if load metrics require |

### 4.5 Module Boundary Rules (Mandatory)

To prevent modular monolith erosion, the following rules apply from Phase 1:

1. **No cross-module database access** — modules own their persistence; other modules reference by identifier only (SKU, Location Code, Order ID).
2. **No direct cross-module domain object imports** — integration via application commands, queries, or domain events only.
3. **Inventory Balance is the sole ATP mutator** — no other module modifies reserved, on-hand, or quarantined quantities directly.
4. **External systems integrate through ACL adapters** — foreign models are translated at the adapter, never in domain entities.
5. **Inventory Intelligence is read-only** — projections consume events; never write back to source aggregates.
6. **Sagas own cross-module workflows** — reservation, transfer, and go-live coordination live in application orchestration, not buried in adapters.

### 4.6 Architecture Decision Record

| Field | Decision |
|-------|----------|
| **ADR ID** | ADR-001 |
| **Title** | Primary Architecture Style Selection |
| **Status** | Proposed |
| **Context** | IMS requires domain-rich inventory platform under fixed budget, limited ops capacity, and 18-month phased delivery with 13 bounded contexts |
| **Decision** | Adopt **Modular Monolith** as deployment topology with **Clean/Hexagonal** internal structure per bounded context module, **internal event-driven** cross-module integration, and **CQRS** for Inventory Intelligence |
| **Consequences** | Single deployable unit; enforced module boundaries required; selective service extraction deferred to Phase 3; team must adopt DDD and ports/adapters discipline |
| **Alternatives rejected** | Layered (insufficient domain alignment); Microservices (premature ops and consistency cost) |

---

## 5. Conclusion

No single architecture style from the comparison list is sufficient on its own for the Inventory Management System.

- **Layered Architecture** is too weak for this domain complexity and is **rejected**.
- **Microservices** is too heavy for MVP constraints and core consistency needs and is **rejected** as the initial topology.
- **Clean Architecture**, **Hexagonal Architecture**, and **Onion Architecture** are **selected together** as the internal organization of each bounded context module — they protect domain rules and external integrations.
- **Modular Monolith** is **selected** as the deployment and system topology — it honors the approved bounded context map, budget, IT capacity, and phased delivery while preserving a credible path to selective service extraction.

The recommended style is documented in SRS-SA-001 (Architecture Vision) and should guide all subsequent solution architecture, technology selection, and detailed design work.

# Business Rules Specification
## Inventory Management System

## Document Information

| Attribute | Detail |
|-----------|--------|
| **Document ID** | SRS-BR-001 |
| **Document Title** | Business Rules — Inventory Management System |
| **Version** | 1.0 |
| **Status** | Draft |
| **Document Owner** | Senior Business Analyst |
